examples.en: The owner shut the dog in the yard.
They built an embankment to hold in the water.
You must not lock a child in a room.
The wizard locks the dragon in a tower.
Don't bottle up your feelings; try talking.
Where is the place where the criminal was locked up?

explain: '가두다'는 '~에 가두다'로 쓰고, 갇히는 쪽은 '갇히다'라고 해요. 사람, 동물, 물, 감정까지 쓸 수 있어요. '넣다'는 그냥 안에 두는 것이고, 가두다는 못 나오게 하는 거예요.
explain_en: 가두다 is used as ~에 가두다, and the one who ends up locked in is expressed with 갇히다. It works for people, animals, water, and even feelings. 넣다 just puts something inside, while 가두다 means making it unable to get out.

examples.en: I tripped on a rock and fell flat on my face.
The child was running, tumbled forward and hurt his knee.
The stock price is suddenly plunging.

examples.ko: 자전거가 급정거하자 몸이 앞으로 고꾸라질 뻔했어요.
examples.en: When the bike stopped suddenly, I almost toppled forward.
I was so sleepy that I fell asleep as if collapsing onto my desk.
The runner took a tumble right before the finish line.

explain: '넘어지다'보다 앞으로 푹 엎어지는 느낌이 강해요. 사람이 쓰러질 때뿐 아니라 주가나 실적이 크게 떨어질 때도 비유로 써요.
explain_en: Compared with '넘어지다', it strongly suggests pitching forward onto one's face. It is also used figuratively when stock prices or results drop sharply.

examples.en: The puppy chewed up my new shoes.
I have a habit of biting my nails when I'm nervous.

examples.ko: 고양이가 소파를 물어뜯지 않게 장난감을 줬어요.
examples.en: I gave the cat a toy so it wouldn't gnaw on the sofa.
The hungry lion tore into the meat.

examples.ko: 볼펜을 자꾸 물어뜯으면 망가질 수 있어요.
examples.en: If you keep chewing on a pen, it can break.
Please don't fight by tearing into each other.

explain: '물다'가 한 번 무는 것이라면, 물어뜯다는 이로 물고 잡아당겨서 떼어 내거나 찢는 거친 동작이에요. 동물이 물건을 망가뜨릴 때, 사람이 손톱·입술을 뜯을 때 써요. 사람끼리 심하게 비난하고 싸울 때도 비유로 써요.
explain_en: If '물다' is a single bite, 물어뜯다 is a rough action of biting and pulling to tear something off or apart. It is used when animals wreck things and when people chew their nails or lips. It also works as a metaphor for people attacking each other harshly.

examples.en: Careless driving leads to accidents.
I was careless and broke a cup.
I opened the door carelessly and hurt my hand.
He is sometimes careless with his words.
I lost points because of a careless mistake.

examples.ko: 약을 부주의하게 두면 아이가 먹을 수 있어요.
examples.en: If you leave medicine carelessly, a child could eat it.

explain: 반대말은 '조심하다', '주의하다'예요. '부주의하다'는 안전 안내문이나 사고 뉴스에서 자주 보이고, 사람에게 직접 쓰면 비판하는 느낌이 강해요. 일상 대화에서는 '덜렁대다'나 '조심성이 없다'를 더 많이 써요.
explain_en: The opposites are '조심하다' and '주의하다'. '부주의하다' appears often in safety notices and accident news, and said directly to a person it sounds quite critical. In daily talk, '덜렁대다' or '조심성이 없다' are more common.

examples.en: A fire broke out on the mountain and the trees are burning.
The old house burned all night.
The blazing sunset dyed the sea red.
The ashes left after the burning blew away in the wind.

examples.ko: 창고가 불탈 뻔했지만 소방관이 불을 껐어요.
examples.en: The warehouse nearly burned, but the firefighters put out the fire.

examples.ko: 불타면 큰일이니까 난로 옆에 종이를 두지 마세요.
examples.en: Don't leave paper next to the heater; it would be serious if it caught fire.

explain: 불타다는 불이 붙어서 타는 거예요. '타다'만 써도 되지만, 불타다는 불이 크게 일어나 활활 타는 모습이 더 잘 보여요. '불타는 노을'처럼 붉게 빛나는 모습에도 써요.
explain_en: 불타다 is to burn with fire. You can use '타다' alone, but 불타다 paints a vivid picture of a fire blazing. It can also describe things glowing red, like '불타는 노을'.

examples.en: In spring, people pick mugwort in the fields.
My grandmother made mugwort soup for me.
Mugwort rice cake has a strong scent, so people either love it or don't.
The smell of mugwort fills the house.

examples.ko: 감기 기운이 있을 때 쑥차를 마셔요.
examples.en: I drink mugwort tea when I feel a cold coming on.
There is even ice cream made from mugwort.

explain: 봄에 캐서 국, 떡, 차로 먹는 풀이에요. 단군 이야기에서 곰이 마늘과 함께 먹은 것으로 나와요. '쑥'은 '쑥 내밀다'처럼 쑥 튀어나오는 모습을 나타내는 부사로도 쓰는데, 소리만 같고 뜻은 달라요.
explain_en: It is a spring plant eaten as soup, rice cake, or tea. In the Dangun myth, the bear eats it together with garlic. There is also an adverb 쑥, as in '쑥 내밀다' (to stick out), which sounds the same but means something different.

examples.en: Yesterday I fell forward on the icy road and hurt my knee.
The child was running happily and fell flat on his face.
I tripped on a stone and almost fell on my face.
The cup tipped over and all the water spilled.
Be careful not to fall on the ice.
Since I fell on the stairs, I walk slowly.

explain: '넘어지다'는 쓰러지는 방향과 상관없이 쓰지만, '엎어지다'는 몸의 앞쪽이 바닥을 향해 앞으로 쓰러질 때 써요. 뒤로 쓰러지면 '자빠지다'를 쓰기도 해요. 컵이나 그릇이 뒤집혀 쏟아질 때도 써요.

phrases.example: 우리 집에서 학교까지는 엎어지면 코 닿을 데예요.
phrases.en: My house is a stone's throw from the school.
phrases.nuance_ko: 아주 가까운 거리를 말할 때 써요.
phrases.nuance_en: Used to say that a place is very close.

explain_en: '넘어지다' can be used for any direction of falling, but '엎어지다' is for falling forward so the front of the body faces the ground. Falling backward can be '자빠지다'. It is also used when a cup or bowl is turned over and spills.

examples.ko: 여름에는 물놀이 중 익사 사고가 늘어요.
examples.en: In summer, drowning accidents during water play increase.

examples.ko: 구명조끼를 입으면 익사를 막을 수 있어요.
examples.en: Wearing a life jacket can prevent drowning.

examples.ko: 아이들 익사 사고가 없도록 어른이 지켜봐야 해요.
examples.en: Adults must watch so that children do not have drowning accidents.
A report of a drowning came on the news.

examples.ko: 익사 위험이 있어서 수영장에 안전 요원이 있어요.
examples.en: There is a risk of drowning, so the pool has lifeguards.
Fortunately, he was rescued just before drowning.

explain: 보통 '익사 사고', '익사 위험'처럼 다른 말과 붙여 써요. 물에 빠졌다가 살았을 때는 '물에 빠지다'를 쓰고, 숨졌을 때 '익사'를 써요. 뉴스와 안전 안내에서 자주 보는 말이에요.
explain_en: It is usually combined with other words, as in '익사 사고' and '익사 위험'. If someone fell in the water but survived, say '물에 빠지다'; '익사' means they died. It is common in news and safety notices.

examples.en: The door slammed shut because of the wind.

examples.ko: 누가 화가 나서 문을 쾅 닫고 나갔어요.
examples.en: Someone got angry and slammed the door on the way out.
Suddenly thunder boomed with a bang.
The car crashed into the wall with a bang.
The heavy box dropped on the floor with a thud.
I woke up startled by the bang.

explain: 크고 무거운 것이 부딪히거나 닫힐 때의 소리를 흉내 내는 말이에요. 같은 소리라도 '탁'은 가볍고, '쿵'은 무겁게 떨어지는 소리, '쾅'은 더 크고 세요. 보통 '쾅 하고', '쾅 소리'로 써요.
explain_en: It imitates the sound of something big and heavy hitting or closing. 탁 is light, 쿵 is a heavy drop, and 쾅 is louder and sharper. Usually used as 쾅 하고 or 쾅 소리.

examples.en: My father saws wood in the yard.
I almost hurt my hand while sawing.

examples.ko: 나무를 반듯하게 톱질하는 게 쉽지 않아요.
examples.en: It's not easy to saw wood straight.
Please put on gloves and saw it.
The carpenter quickly sawed the board.

examples.ko: 주말마다 아버지와 같이 톱질하며 의자를 만들어요.
examples.en: Every weekend I make a chair with my father, sawing together.

explain: 톱으로 나무 같은 것을 자르는 동작이에요. 일상에서는 '톱으로 자르다'라고도 많이 말하지만 '톱질하다'는 톱을 앞뒤로 움직이는 동작 자체에 초점이 있어요. '톱질을 하다'처럼 명사 '톱질'과 '하다'를 띄어 쓰기도 해요.
explain_en: This is the action of cutting something such as wood with a saw. In daily talk people also say '톱으로 자르다', but '톱질하다' focuses on the back-and-forth motion of sawing itself. It can also be split as the noun '톱질' plus '하다', as in '톱질을 하다'.

examples.en: The ball hit the wall and bounced back.
I flicked the marble with my finger.
If you pluck a guitar string, it makes a sound.
The stone skipped across the water.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 일부러 튕기는 것 같아요.
examples.en: She seems to be playing hard to get on purpose.
Raindrops bounced off the umbrella and wet my clothes.

explain: '튀다'와 비슷하지만 '튕기다'는 손가락이나 줄을 세게 쳐서 퉁 하고 움직이게 할 때도 써요. 사람에게 쓰면 관심 있으면서도 일부러 쉽게 받아 주지 않는 모습을 말해요.

phrases.nuance_ko: 관심이 있어도 일부러 바로 받아 주지 않는 모습을 말하는 구어체예요.
phrases.nuance_en: Colloquial: refusing or delaying on purpose despite being interested.

explain_en: Similar to 튀다, but 튕기다 also covers flicking a finger or plucking a string. Said of a person, it means acting hard to get on purpose even though they are interested.

examples.en: The plan is given up halfway.
That business was finally abandoned.
I took out a dream that had been given up.

examples.ko: 시간이 없으면 일부는 포기될 수 있어요.
examples.en: If time is short, some may be given up.
Several plans are being dropped.
The construction was dropped, so the land is empty.

explain: 계획, 사업, 공사처럼 하던 일이 끝까지 가지 못하고 멈췄을 때 써요. 사람이 스스로 그만두는 건 '포기하다'예요. 일이 멈췄다는 뜻으로 '중단되다'도 많이 써요. 일상 대화에서는 '포기하다'를 훨씬 많이 써요.
explain_en: Used when a plan, business or construction project stops before it is finished. A person quitting by choice uses the active verb. The verb for 'be suspended' is also common for stopped projects. In daily talk the active verb is far more common.

examples.en: The enemy army finally declared surrender.
Okay, I give up. I lost.
When his strength ran out, he surrendered.
The news of the surrender was broadcast on the radio.
My sibling could not stand the tickling and gave in.
We will not surrender to the end.

explain: '항복하다'로 동사처럼 쓰고, 장난으로 "항복!"이라고 외치기도 해요. 비슷한 '굴복하다'는 힘이나 압력에 눌려 따르는 거고, '항복'은 싸움이나 승부에서 졌다고 인정하는 거예요.
explain_en: It is used as a verb with '하다' ('항복하다'), and people also shout '항복!' as a joke when they give up. The similar '굴복하다' (yield) is about bowing to power or pressure, while '항복' is about admitting defeat in a fight or contest.

en: be bewitched; be lured; be spellbound

examples.en: I was completely spellbound by that singer's voice.

examples.ko: 저는 뭐에 홀린 것처럼 가게에 들어갔어요.
examples.en: I walked into the shop as if I were under a spell.

examples.ko: 예쁜 광고에 홀려서 비싼 가방을 샀어요.
examples.en: I got lured by a pretty ad and bought an expensive bag.
People stared as if they were entranced by the magic.
Don't let yourself be taken in by sweet words.
Anyone would be charmed by that actor's smile.

explain: 홀리다는 무엇에 마음을 빼앗겨 정신을 못 차리는 모습이에요. '뭐에 홀린 것 같다'는 이유를 모르겠는데 이상하게 끌려갔을 때 자주 해요. '반하다'가 좋아하는 마음이라면 홀리다는 정신이 나간 듯한 느낌이 더 강해요.

phrases.example: 제가 왜 그걸 샀는지 모르겠어요. 뭐에 홀린 것 같아요.
phrases.en: I feel like I was possessed.
phrases.nuance_ko: 자기가 한 행동이 이해되지 않을 때 쓰는 말이에요. 귀신이 씐 것처럼 정신이 없었다는 비유예요.
phrases.nuance_en: Said when you cannot understand your own action, as if something took control of you.
phrases.en_equiv: I don't know what came over me.

explain_en: 홀리다 describes losing your head because something has captured your attention. '뭐에 홀린 것 같다' is a common line when you did something strange without knowing why. 반하다 is about falling for someone, while 홀리다 feels more like being in a trance.
